audience: Beginning linear algebra students working in the plane R^2. They have seen linear maps as motions of the grid and know that a matrix records where the two basis vectors land; they have not yet multiplied two matrices.
assumed: A linear map moves the grid so that lines stay straight, parallel and evenly spaced, with the origin fixed
The columns of a matrix are the landing spots of e1 and e2
Applying a matrix to a vector: A v = x·(column 1) + y·(column 2)
What the quarter-turn R and the shear S each do to the grid on their own
central_question: If we do one linear map and then another, which single matrix describes the whole motion, and does it matter which map goes first?
opening: A dark frame with the untransformed grid of the plane in the left two thirds, the green arrow e1 and the red arrow e2 at the origin with their labels, and a yellow sample vector v. The right third is empty.

scenes.title: Two motions in a row
scenes.purpose: Doing a rotation and then a shear produces one overall motion of the grid, and that overall motion is again linear, so it must have a matrix of its own.
scenes.shows: The matrices R (blue) and S (gold) fade into the text area, one below the other. The letter R brightens while the whole plane turns a quarter-turn as one calm motion; grid, e1, e2 and v all ride along. After a hold, the letter S brightens and the already rotated plane is sheared. After another hold, the plane is undone smoothly back to the starting grid. It is then replayed with no pause in the middle, as one continuous motion from start to finish: the grid lines visibly stay straight, parallel and evenly spaced the whole way, and the origin never moves. The yellow v ends at the same spot as in the two-stage version. The viewer is left with a transformed grid that looks like the result of any single linear map and has no matrix yet.
key_points: First the rotation acts on the plane, then the shear acts on what the rotation produced
The sample vector v is carried through both stages to one final position
Replayed as one motion, the grid lines stay straight, parallel and evenly spaced, and the origin stays fixed
A linear motion must have a matrix; its place in the text area is still empty
elements: grid: the plane, now in the state after rotation then shear
e1: green first basis vector, carried by both motions
e2: red second basis vector, carried by both motions
v: yellow sample vector at its final position
matrix R: blue rotation matrix in the text area
matrix S: gold shear matrix in the text area
scenes.ends_with: The grid rests in its final state after rotation then shear, with e1, e2 and v at their landing positions and labelled. The text area holds the blue matrix R above the gold matrix S, with empty space below them.

interactive.label: progress
interactive.changes: Scrubs the two-stage motion of the whole plane from the starting grid (0), through the rotated grid (middle), to the rotated-then-sheared grid (end); default is the end state
interactive.discover: At every moment of the combined motion the grid is still made of straight, parallel, evenly spaced lines through a fixed origin

interactive.label: v: x
interactive.changes: The first coordinate of the sample vector v before the motions, over a few grid units either side of the origin; v's final position updates through the real maps
interactive.discover: Every starting vector is carried to its own definite end point by the same combined motion

scenes.title: Reading off the matrix
scenes.purpose: The matrix of the combined motion is read off like any other matrix: its columns are the final landing spots of e1 and e2.
scenes.shows: The plane is undone smoothly to the starting grid and v dims. The two-stage motion plays again, and this time e1 and e2 each leave a faint muted trail with a small dot at the intermediate stop. e1 turns upright and is then pushed sideways by the shear. e2 turns to lie along the horizontal axis, and the shear then leaves it exactly where it is. An empty pair of brackets appears in the text area below R and S. The coordinates of e1's tip travel from the arrow into the first column in green, then those of e2 into the second column in red. As a check, v brightens again and the new matrix is applied to v's original coordinates as a short column computation in the text area. The result is the point where v already sits, and that point pulses once. The computation and the trails then fade out.
key_points: Only e1 and e2 need to be followed; each makes two moves with a visible stop in between
The shear moves the rotated e1 but leaves the rotated e2 in place
The final coordinates of e1 and e2 become the first and second column of one matrix
That one matrix sends v straight to the place the two motions took it
elements: grid: the plane in the state after rotation then shear
e1: green first basis vector at its final position
e2: red second basis vector at its final position
v: yellow sample vector at its final position
matrix R: blue rotation matrix in the text area
matrix S: gold shear matrix in the text area
combined matrix: unnamed matrix with a green first column and a red second column, below R and S
scenes.ends_with: The transformed grid with e1, e2 and v at their final positions; trails, stop markers and the check computation are gone. The text area shows R, S and below them the still unnamed combined matrix with a green and a red column.

interactive.label: progress
interactive.changes: Scrubs the plane and the trails of e1 and e2 from the starting grid, through the stop after the rotation, to the final grid; default is the final grid
interactive.discover: The columns of the combined matrix are exactly where the two arrows are at the far end of the slider, and each arrow passes through a clear halfway stop

scenes.title: The product SR, read right to left
scenes.purpose: The combined matrix is called the product SR, defined by (SR) v = S(R v); the matrix written next to v acts first, so the order reads right to left.
scenes.shows: The expression S(R v) is written in the text area with yellow v innermost, blue R wrapped around it and gold S wrapped around that, so the brackets read as nested shells. The plane is undone smoothly to the starting grid. During the rotation the inner shell and the letter R glow, and a small 1 appears under R. During the shear the outer shell and the letter S glow, and a small 2 appears under S. The glow has therefore swept from right to left across the formula while the motions happened in time order. After a hold, the brackets slide so that S and R sit together as (SR) v, joined to S(R v) by an equals sign. The letters SR turn purple and travel to the unnamed combined matrix, where they become its name in front of an equals sign, and its brackets turn purple.
key_points: v is touched first by the matrix directly next to it, R, and only then by S
The numbers 1 and 2 under R and S mark the time order, which runs right to left in the written product
(SR) v = S(R v): the product is defined as the single matrix that does both steps
The matrix read off from the basis vectors is this product SR
elements: grid: the plane in the state after rotation then shear
e1: green first basis vector at its final position
e2: red second basis vector at its final position
v: yellow sample vector at its final position
matrix R: blue rotation matrix in the text area
matrix S: gold shear matrix in the text area
order formula: (SR) v = S(R v) with a small 1 under R and a small 2 under S
product SR: the combined matrix, now named SR in purple, with green and red columns
scenes.ends_with: The transformed grid with e1, e2 and v. The text area shows R, S, the order formula (SR) v = S(R v) with the marks 1 and 2 under R and S, and the purple-named matrix SR with its green and red columns.

interactive.label: progress
interactive.changes: Scrubs the plane through the rotation and then the shear, and the glow in the formula follows it: R is lit during the first half, S during the second; default is the final state
interactive.discover: Moving forward in time lights the formula from right to left: the letter nearest v always acts first

scenes.title: Column by column
scenes.purpose: Each column of SR is S applied to the matching column of R; in general, column i of BA is B times column i of A.
scenes.shows: v and the order formula fade out. The shear alone is undone smoothly, so the plane rests in the rotated state. The two arrows now sit exactly on the columns of R: the first column of the blue matrix R glows green together with e1, then the second glows red together with e2, so the halfway stops are recognised as the columns of R. In the text area the matrices rearrange into one line, S times R equals SR. The shear is then applied to the plane again, slowly. As e1 moves, a short column computation shows S acting on the green column alone, and the result slides into the first column of SR. The same happens for the red column, which the shear leaves unchanged. After a hold, the letters are relabelled in place to the general statement B [a1 | a2] = [B a1 | B a2], with a1 green and a2 red, and the concrete product stays above it. The single-column computations fade.
key_points: After the first map, e1 and e2 sit on the columns of R
The second map S is then applied to each of those columns separately
Each result is the matching column of SR
General rule: column i of BA = B times column i of A; the left matrix acts on the columns of the right one
elements: grid: the plane in the state after rotation then shear
e1: green first basis vector at its final position
e2: red second basis vector at its final position
product equation: S · R = SR written with all three matrices, columns of R and SR in green and red
column rule: B [a1 | a2] = [B a1 | B a2] with a1 green and a2 red
scenes.ends_with: The grid in its final state after rotation then shear, with only e1 and e2 on it. The text area shows the product equation S · R = SR with coloured columns, and below it the general column rule.

interactive.label: shear
interactive.changes: The strength of the shear S, from no shear to about twice the storyboarded amount; the sheared plane, the entry in S and the columns of SR all update together; default is the storyboarded shear
interactive.discover: Whatever the shear, each column of SR is that shear applied to the corresponding column of R: the first column changes with the slider, the second never does

scenes.title: Not entry by entry
scenes.purpose: Multiplying matching entries does not give the product: that matrix describes a completely different motion from the one we watched.
scenes.shows: Below the product equation, a muted matrix is assembled by pairing each entry of S with the entry of R in the same position; the four pairs light up one at a time and their products drop into place. The plane is then moved slowly from the SR state to the state this muted matrix describes, by blending the matrix entries. The grid squeezes flat until every grid line and both basis arrows lie on a single line through the origin, with e1 shrunk to the origin itself. The picture is held: this collapsed plane is clearly not the rotated and sheared grid. The plane is then moved back just as slowly to the SR state, the muted matrix fades out, and the purple SR briefly brightens as the grid returns to it.
key_points: An entry-by-entry 'product' is easy to write down
Its grid collapses onto a line, so it is not the motion 'rotate, then shear'
The true product is the one whose columns follow the basis vectors through both motions
elements: grid: the plane back in the state after rotation then shear
e1: green first basis vector at its final position
e2: red second basis vector at its final position
product equation: S · R = SR with coloured columns
column rule: B [a1 | a2] = [B a1 | B a2]
scenes.ends_with: Exactly the picture from the end of the previous scene: the grid after rotation then shear with e1 and e2, and in the text area the product equation S · R = SR and the column rule. The muted entrywise matrix is gone.

interactive.label: matrix
interactive.changes: Chooses which matrix the plane shows: 'SR' (default, the true product) or 'entrywise' (the muted matrix); the plane blends smoothly between the two states
interactive.discover: Only the column-rule product reproduces the motion; the entrywise matrix flattens the whole plane onto a line

scenes.title: The other order
scenes.purpose: Doing the same two motions in the opposite order, shear first and then rotation, ends in a different grid and gives a different matrix RS.
scenes.shows: The column rule fades and the product equation contracts to the purple matrix SR alone. The plane shrinks calmly into the left half of the geometry area, with a purple label SR beside it, and is undone smoothly to the starting grid. A second, identical starting plane with its own e1 and e2 fades in slowly in the right half, labelled RS in teal. Both planes then run in sync. In the first stage the left one rotates while the right one shears. After a pause, in the second stage the left one shears while the right one rotates. Faint trails with stop dots follow all four basis arrows. On the right, e1 is not moved at all by the shear and is then turned upright, and e2 is first tipped over by the shear and then turned. The coordinates of the right-hand arrows drop into a new teal-bracketed matrix RS in the text area, beside SR. After a hold, the two planes slide together until they overlap, the left grid tinted purple and the right grid tinted teal. The origins and axes coincide, but the grid lines and both pairs of basis arrows point to different places. They slide apart again, the trails fade, and a ≠ sign fades in between the two matrices.
key_points: Same two maps, same starting grid, only the order differs
The right-hand basis arrows take different routes and stop at different places
Reading their landing spots gives RS, whose columns differ from those of SR
Laid over each other, the two final grids do not match: SR ≠ RS
elements: left plane: small grid in the state after rotation then shear, tinted purple, labelled SR
right plane: small grid in the state after shear then rotation, tinted teal, labelled RS
e1: green first basis vector, one in each plane at its own final position
e2: red second basis vector, one in each plane at its own final position
product SR: purple-named matrix with green and red columns
product RS: teal-named matrix with green and red columns
not-equal sign: ≠ between SR and RS in the text area
scenes.ends_with: Two small planes side by side in the geometry area: on the left the purple-tinted final grid of 'rotation then shear' labelled SR, on the right the teal-tinted final grid of 'shear then rotation' labelled RS, each with its own e1 and e2. The text area shows the matrices SR and RS with a ≠ between them.

interactive.label: progress
interactive.changes: Scrubs both planes in sync from the common starting grid, through their different halfway states, to their final grids; default is the final state
interactive.discover: The two planes already differ at the halfway stop and never come back together

interactive.label: overlay
interactive.changes: Slides the two planes smoothly on top of each other in their purple and teal tints, or apart again; default is apart
interactive.discover: With the origins on top of each other, the grid lines and basis arrows of the two orders clearly land in different places

scenes.title: Why the order matters
scenes.purpose: The order matters because the second map acts on whatever the first one produced: the shear moves a vector that has height but leaves a vector on the horizontal axis alone.
scenes.shows: Both planes are undone smoothly to the starting grid, and in each plane e2 and the grid dim slightly so that the green e1 stands out. The first stage plays in both planes. On the left, e1 turns upright. On the right, the shear runs, the grid visibly slides, and e1 stays lying on the horizontal axis and does not move. After a hold, the second stage plays. On the left, the shear now meets an upright e1, and its tip is carried sideways along a horizontal grid line, which is highlighted briefly. On the right, the rotation turns the untouched e1 upright. The two green arrows end in different places, and the green first columns of SR and RS brighten together in the text area to show the same difference in numbers. The dimming is lifted and the highlight fades.
key_points: The shear pushes points sideways in proportion to their height
Applied first, the shear finds e1 on the axis with no height, and nothing happens to it
Applied second, the shear finds e1 already turned upright and pushes it sideways
The same map does different things because it is fed different inputs, which is why the first columns of SR and RS differ
elements: left plane: small purple-tinted grid after rotation then shear, labelled SR
right plane: small teal-tinted grid after shear then rotation, labelled RS
e1: green first basis vector, one in each plane at its own final position
e2: red second basis vector, one in each plane at its own final position
product SR: purple-named matrix with green and red columns
product RS: teal-named matrix with green and red columns
not-equal sign: ≠ between SR and RS in the text area
scenes.ends_with: The same side-by-side picture as before: the purple-tinted SR grid on the left and the teal-tinted RS grid on the right at full brightness, each with e1 and e2, and in the text area the matrices SR and RS with ≠ between them.

interactive.label: shear
interactive.changes: The strength of the shear S in both planes, from no shear to about twice the storyboarded amount; both final grids and the entries of SR and RS update; default is the storyboarded shear
interactive.discover: The stronger the shear, the further apart the two results; only with no shear at all do the two orders agree

scenes.title: In general, not always
scenes.purpose: AB ≠ BA in general, but some pairs do commute, for example two rotations; the rule to keep is that BA means first A, then B.
scenes.shows: Both planes are undone smoothly to the starting grid. In the labels and in the text area the gold S is replaced by a white T, a second rotation by a smaller angle; the plane labels become TR and RT, and the two matrices fade to empty brackets. The planes play in sync. On the left the quarter-turn runs and then the small turn; on the right the small turn runs and then the quarter-turn. Both grids end in visibly the same position. The planes slide together and overlap perfectly, the purple and teal grid lines lying exactly on each other, while the brackets fill with identical columns and the ≠ turns into =. After a long hold, the planes slide apart and are undone to the starting grid, and T is replaced by S again. The shear and rotation replay in both orders one last time, ending in the two different grids with SR ≠ RS. Finally the general order formula (BA) v = B(A v) fades in at the top of the text area, with a small 1 under A and a small 2 under B.
key_points: Two rotations done in either order end in the same grid, so their products are equal
With the shear back in place, the two orders again end in different grids
So AB ≠ BA is the usual case, not a law without exceptions
(BA) v = B(A v): BA always means first A, then B
elements: left plane: small purple-tinted grid after rotation then shear, labelled SR
right plane: small teal-tinted grid after shear then rotation, labelled RS
e1: green first basis vector, one in each plane at its own final position
e2: red second basis vector, one in each plane at its own final position
product SR: purple-named matrix with green and red columns
product RS: teal-named matrix with green and red columns
not-equal sign: ≠ between SR and RS in the text area
order formula: (BA) v = B(A v) with a small 1 under A and a small 2 under B
scenes.ends_with: The two different final grids side by side, purple-tinted SR on the left and teal-tinted RS on the right, each with e1 and e2. The text area shows the general order formula (BA) v = B(A v) with the marks 1 under A and 2 under B at the top, and below it the matrices SR and RS with ≠ between them. The frame holds still.

interactive.label: second map
interactive.changes: Chooses the partner of the quarter-turn R in both planes: 'shear' (default, the film's example, as at the start and end of the scene), 'small turn' or 'uniform scaling'; both planes replay smoothly with the chosen map in the two orders, and the sign between the matrices shows = or ≠
interactive.discover: The shear does not commute with the rotation, while another rotation or a uniform scaling does: whether order matters depends on the pair

interactive.label: overlay
interactive.changes: Slides the two planes smoothly on top of each other in their purple and teal tints, or apart again; default is apart
interactive.discover: For a commuting pair the two grids coincide exactly; for the shear they do not

teaching_plan.learning_goal: The student can explain that the product BA is the single matrix of the motion 'first A, then B', can compute it by following where e1 and e2 land (column i of BA = B times column i of A), and can show with the rotation R and shear S why swapping the order usually gives a different matrix.
prerequisites: A linear map of the plane moves the grid so that lines stay straight, parallel and evenly spaced, and the origin stays fixed
The columns of a matrix are the landing spots of e1 and e2
Applying a matrix to a vector: A v = x·(column 1) + y·(column 2) for v = (x, y)
What the 90° rotation R = [[0,-1],[1,0]] and the shear S = [[1,1],[0,1]] do to the grid (S sends (x, y) to (x+y, y))
teaching_plan.key_insight: A matrix product is not a new arithmetic rule but a recording of two motions played one after the other: BA is the one matrix whose columns show where e1 and e2 end up after first A, then B. Because motions done in a different order end in a different place, AB and BA are usually different matrices.
misconceptions: BA means 'first B, then A' because we read left to right (in fact the matrix next to the vector acts first: B(A v))
Matrices are multiplied entry by entry, like adding them
Order does not matter, as with ordinary numbers: AB = BA
The product is just a memorised row-times-column recipe with no geometric meaning
In the column rule, mixing up which matrix acts on which columns (taking A times the columns of B to get BA)
Overcorrection: matrices never commute (some pairs do, for example two rotations)
teaching_plan.concrete_example: The quarter-turn R = [[0,-1],[1,0]] and the shear S = [[1,1],[0,1]] acting on the grid of R^2, with e1 and e2 as two coloured arrows. First rotate, then shear: e1 goes (1,0) → (0,1) → (1,1) and e2 goes (0,1) → (-1,0) → (-1,0), so SR = [[1,-1],[1,0]]. Then the opposite order, first shear, then rotate: e1 goes (1,0) → (1,0) → (0,1) and e2 goes (0,1) → (1,1) → (-1,1), so RS = [[0,-1],[1,1]]. The two final grids are visibly different.

arc.step: Doing two linear maps in a row (rotate, then shear) produces one overall motion of the grid, and that motion is itself linear.
arc.why_now: It starts from what the student already knows (single linear maps as grid motions) and raises the film's question: if the result is linear, it must have a matrix. Which one?
arc.visual_idea: Play R on the grid, pause, then play S on the already-rotated grid. Then fade out the intermediate stage and replay start → end as a single smooth motion: the grid lines are still straight, parallel and evenly spaced, and the origin is fixed. A sample vector v = (2,1) rides along: (2,1) → (-1,2) → (1,2).

arc.step: The matrix of the combined motion is read off like any other: follow e1 and e2 to their final positions. Here e1 lands at (1,1) and e2 at (-1,0), giving [[1,-1],[1,0]].
arc.why_now: It uses only the prerequisite 'columns are where the basis vectors land', now applied to the composite. The student gets the answer concretely before any notation or rule appears.
arc.visual_idea: Replay the two-stage motion with only the green e1 and red e2 highlighted, each leaving a faint trail with its intermediate stop marked: e1 (1,0) → (0,1) → (1,1), e2 (0,1) → (-1,0) → (-1,0). The final coordinates drop into the columns of an empty matrix. Check: this matrix applied to (2,1) gives (1,2), the same point the vector reached in step 1.

arc.step: This matrix gets a name: the product SR, defined by (SR) v = S(R v). The order reads right to left, because R sits next to v and touches it first.
arc.why_now: The object has now been seen, so it can be named. The order convention must be fixed here, before the general rule and before the order is swapped, or everything after is ambiguous.
arc.visual_idea: Write S(R v) with the brackets drawn as nested shells around v. As the animation plays, the inner R lights up during the rotation and the outer S during the shear, a highlight sweeping right to left. Then the brackets slide away to leave (SR) v, with small labels '1st' under R and '2nd' under S.

arc.step: Column rule: each intermediate stop in step 2 was a column of R, and S was then applied to it. So column i of SR = S times column i of R, and in general column i of BA = B times column i of A.
arc.why_now: This turns the watched trails into a general computation. It needs the trails from step 2 and the name and order from step 3.
arc.visual_idea: Freeze after the rotation: the two arrows sit exactly on the columns of R, which glow in the matrix R. Then S grabs each column separately: S·(0,1) = (1,1) and S·(-1,0) = (-1,0), each result sliding into its column of SR. Generalise by relabelling to B·[a1 | a2] = [B a1 | B a2]. Briefly flash the entrywise 'product' of S and R, [[0,-1],[0,0]], and show its grid collapsing onto a line. That is plainly not the motion we watched, so it is discarded.

arc.step: Running the same two motions in the opposite order, shear first and then rotate, gives a different final grid and a different matrix: RS = [[0,-1],[1,1]].
arc.why_now: With the convention and the column rule in hand, the student can predict RS and then watch it. This is the central moment, which the earlier steps prepared.
arc.visual_idea: Split screen from the same starting grid. Left: R then S, labelled SR. Right: S then R, labelled RS, with trails e1 (1,0) → (1,0) → (0,1) and e2 (0,1) → (1,1) → (-1,1). Both sides run in sync and stop. Overlay the two final grids in different tints: the basis arrows point to different places, (1,1), (-1,0) versus (0,1), (-1,1). The matrices [[1,-1],[1,0]] and [[0,-1],[1,1]] appear below with a ≠ between them.

arc.step: In general AB ≠ BA, because the second motion acts on whatever the first one produced. 'In general' still allows exceptions: some pairs do commute.
arc.why_now: It consolidates the insight by explaining why the order mattered here and marks the boundary of the claim, so the student does not overgeneralise to 'never equal'.
arc.visual_idea: Zoom on e1 in both halves. On the left the shear acts on a rotated e1, which now has height and gets pushed sideways. On the right the shear acts on the original e1, which lies on the x-axis and does not move. Then a short contrast: two rotations (R and a 45° turn) played in both orders side by side, and the final grids coincide exactly, tagged 'sometimes equal'. End on the line 'BA = first A, then B' above the two different R/S grids.

context.source_title: Linear Algebra, Lecture 3: Linear maps, matrices and determinants
context.topic_summary: Multiplying matrices means doing one linear map after another. BA means 'first A, then B', and each column of BA is B applied to the matching column of A. Because order matters for motions, AB ≠ BA in general.
